sharp/recall: Back to cats like fish. Fish's query gave cats a score of two, like zero, and itself one. Softmax turned those into soft weights: mostly cats, some of the rest.
sharp/long: Those queries and keys had two entries each; Vaswani's had sixty four. A dot product adds one product per entry, so longer vectors tend to give bigger scores.
sharp/bigger: Make the scores four times bigger: eight, zero and four. Their gaps grow just as much, and softmax goes all or nothing: nearly all the weight lands on cats.
sharp/nudge: Now nudge fish's score up by a half, in both. The soft weights shift. The sharp ones barely move.
sharp/flat: How far the weights move for a nudge is their slope: the gradient that backprop carries to the queries and keys. Near zero, they have almost nothing to learn from. The softmax is saturated, like a sigmoid far from zero.
sharp/britz: In 2017, Denny Britz and colleagues found long vectors hurting translation. With queries and keys of a thousand and twenty four numbers, dot-product attention did much worse than with five hundred and twelve.
sharp/vaswani: Months later, Ashish Vaswani and colleagues suspected why: large dot products, they wrote, push the softmax into regions where it has extremely small gradients.
why/coin: Why do longer vectors give bigger scores? Picture a query and a key whose entries are plus or minus one, at random. Each product in their dot product is then also plus or minus one: a coin flip.
why/walk: Add the flips one at a time, and the running total takes a walk, up one or down one. Here are many walks of sixty four steps.
why/cancel: Ups and downs mostly cancel, but rarely exactly. The longer the walk, the farther from zero it tends to end, yet nowhere near the sixty four it could reach.
why/count: Now count exactly, with just four flips. They can land sixteen ways, and their sums run from minus four to four, zero most often.
why/square: Pluses and minuses would cancel in an average, so measure size by squaring. The sixteen squares average exactly four: d k itself.
why/typical: The square root of that, two, is a typical size: how far from zero a score usually lands.
why/grow: At any length, the average square is d k, so a typical score lands about the square root of d k from zero. Sixty four flips give about eight: sixteen times the flips, only four times the size.
why/footnote: Vaswani's paper makes this same argument, in a footnote.
scale/fix: So divide every score by the square root of d k. A typical score then lands about one from zero, however long the vectors.
scale/root: Why the square root, and not d k itself? Divide by d k, and long vectors' scores shrink toward zero, and every weight toward an equal share.
scale/name: Vaswani's team called this scaled dot-product attention, and the name is the recipe: a dot product, scaled down by the square root of d k.
scale/dot: Try it with four entries each. The dot product of these two is two, plus zero, plus zero, plus two: four.
scale/divide: Here d k is four, and its square root is two, so the score is four over two: two.
scale/row: Scale the dot products with all three keys the same way. Four, zero and two become two, zero and one: the soft scores we began with.
scale/soft: Softmax gives the soft weights again, about two thirds on the first key, and a nudge still moves them.
